subChunks.title: Chemical Reactions — Equilibrium, Kinetics & Thermodynamics

storyBeats.txt: Theodora poured two clear solutions together. They turned vivid yellow, then faded back toward pale gold over several minutes. "You are watching a reaction find its equilibrium," she said. "The world does not simply react — it negotiates. The forward reaction and the reverse reaction reach a balance, and that balance tells you the ratio of products to reactants at which the system is content to rest."

"But knowing the equilibrium position tells you nothing about how quickly you will get there. That is kinetics — the study of reaction rates, of activation energies, of why some reactions that are thermodynamically favourable take millions of years to occur without a catalyst."

"And underlying everything — the question of whether a reaction wants to happen at all — is thermodynamics. The universe tends toward states of lower energy and greater disorder. When these drives cooperate, reactions are spontaneous. When they conflict, temperature becomes the deciding factor. Understand these three frameworks and you understand what happens in a reaction, how fast, and whether nature endorses it at all."

subChunks.hookHtml: Chemical reactions are governed by three interlocking frameworks: thermodynamics (whether a reaction is energetically favourable), kinetics (how fast a reaction proceeds), and equilibrium (the balance point between forward and reverse reactions). These frameworks are distinct — a thermodynamically favourable reaction may be kinetically inert (diamonds converting to graphite is thermodynamically spontaneous but imperceptibly slow), and a reaction at equilibrium is not static but involves constant forward and reverse transformations. Together, they explain how industrial processes like the Haber-Bosch synthesis of ammonia are designed and optimised.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Thermodynamics — Enthalpy, Entropy, and Gibbs Energy

Enthalpy (H): The heat content of a system at constant pressure. ΔH = H_products − H_reactants. Exothermic reactions: ΔH < 0 (heat released). Endothermic: ΔH > 0 (heat absorbed). ΔH can be calculated from bond energies (bonds broken − bonds formed) or Hess's Law (path-independent).

Entropy (S): A measure of disorder or dispersal of energy. ΔS > 0 when disorder increases (e.g. gas produced from solids, dissolving, mixing). Second Law: total entropy of the universe always increases in a spontaneous process.

Gibbs Free Energy (G): The thermodynamic criterion for spontaneity: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔG < 0: reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable). ΔG > 0: non-spontaneous. ΔG = 0: system is at equilibrium. Temperature determines which term dominates when ΔH and ΔS have opposing effects.

Four combinations: (1) ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 → always spontaneous; (2) ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 → never spontaneous; (3) ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0 → spontaneous at low T; (4) ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → spontaneous at high T.

Chemical Equilibrium

Most reactions are reversible. At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, and concentrations remain constant (though not necessarily equal). The equilibrium constant K_c expresses the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations (each raised to their stoichiometric power) at equilibrium:

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b)

K > 1: products favoured. K < 1: reactants favoured. K is temperature-dependent only.

The reaction quotient Q has the same form but uses any concentrations, not necessarily equilibrium ones. If Q < K: reaction proceeds forward. If Q > K: reaction proceeds reverse.

Le Chatelier's Principle: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to partially counteract the disturbance. Changes that shift equilibrium:

  • Concentration: Adding reactant → shifts forward; adding product → shifts reverse.
  • Pressure (for gases): Increasing pressure → shifts toward fewer moles of gas.
  • Temperature: Increasing temperature → shifts in the endothermic direction; decreasing → exothermic direction. (Note: temperature changes K; other factors only shift Q toward K.)
  • Catalyst: Does NOT shift equilibrium — increases rates of both forward and reverse equally; equilibrium is reached faster but K is unchanged.

Acid-Base Equilibria

Brønsted-Lowry definition: Acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor. In water: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻. K_a = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. pK_a = −log(K_a). Lower pK_a = stronger acid.

pH = −log[H⁺]. For strong acids: [H⁺] = initial concentration. For weak acids: quadratic or approximation (if Ka << C). Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH + pOH = 14.

Buffer solutions: Resist pH change on addition of acid or alkali. Consist of weak acid + its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

Reaction Kinetics

Rate of reaction: Change in concentration per unit time. Rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt = +Δ[product]/Δt.

Rate equation: Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant, and m, n are orders of reaction (determined experimentally, not from stoichiometry). Overall order = m + n.

Factors affecting rate:

  • Temperature: Higher T → more molecules have energy ≥ activation energy E_a. Arrhenius equation: k = A e^(−E_a/RT). Rule of thumb: 10°C rise roughly doubles many reaction rates.
  • Concentration/pressure: More frequent collisions.
  • Surface area: Solid reactants — smaller particles = more surface.
  • Catalyst: Lowers activation energy E_a by providing an alternative mechanism. Enzyme catalysts are highly specific and efficient.

Activation energy and collision theory: Collisions must have correct orientation and energy ≥ E_a to react. Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: only the tail of the distribution has energy ≥ E_a. Temperature shifts the distribution, greatly increasing the fraction above E_a.

The Haber Process — Industrial Application

N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (exothermic). Industrial conditions: 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst.

Analysis via Le Chatelier: High pressure favours NH₃ (4 mol gas → 2 mol). Low temperature favours NH₃ (exothermic, cooler → forward) but gives a very slow rate. The compromise: 450°C is high enough for acceptable rate; the catalyst (Fe/K₂O/Al₂O₃) dramatically lowers E_a, giving sufficient rate without needing very high temperature. The yield (≈15% at equilibrium at 450°C) is increased by removing NH₃ continuously and recycling unreacted gases — a process engineering solution to a thermodynamic constraint.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a catalyst makes a reaction go faster without being used up, and why it doesn't change where the equilibrium ends up.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Consider the reaction: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). ΔH = +57 kJ/mol. The equilibrium constant K_c = 4.64 × 10⁻³ mol/L at 25°C. (1) Is this reaction endothermic or exothermic? What does the positive ΔH tell you about equilibrium position relative to temperature? (2) Write the expression for K_c for this reaction. (3) In a 2.0 L vessel, at equilibrium there are 0.0400 mol N₂O₄ and 0.0600 mol NO₂. Calculate K_c. (4) If the pressure on the system is increased by halving the volume, in which direction does equilibrium shift? Explain using Le Chatelier's Principle. (5) If the temperature is increased, does K_c increase or decrease? Explain.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Positive ΔH = endothermic — heat is absorbed in the forward reaction. Since increasing temperature drives equilibrium in the endothermic direction (forward), higher temperature increases the proportion of NO₂ and increases K_c. At 25°C, K_c is small (reactants moderately favoured).

(2) K_c = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄]

(3) Concentrations: [N₂O₄] = 0.0400/2.0 = 0.0200 mol/L; [NO₂] = 0.0600/2.0 = 0.0300 mol/L. K_c = (0.0300)² / (0.0200) = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.0200 = 0.0450 mol/L. (Note: this differs from the given 4.64 × 10⁻³ at 25°C, indicating the system is at a different temperature — the calculation is valid for whatever temperature gives this equilibrium composition.)

(4) Halving volume doubles concentrations. Forward reaction: 1 mol gas → 2 mol gas (N₂O₄ → 2NO₂). Le Chatelier: increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward fewer moles of gas — the reverse direction (toward N₂O₄). This partially relieves the pressure increase by reducing the total number of gas molecules.

(5) Since the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH > 0), increasing temperature shifts equilibrium to the right (more NO₂). This means K_c increases with temperature for endothermic reactions. For exothermic reactions, K_c decreases with temperature. Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of K — concentration and pressure changes shift Q toward K but do not change K itself.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The Contact Process manufactures sulfuric acid. The key equilibrium step is: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. Industrial conditions: 450°C, 1–2 atm, vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst. (1) Using Le Chatelier's Principle, explain the effect on yield of: (a) increasing temperature; (b) increasing pressure; (c) adding more O₂. (2) If high pressure favours SO₃, why is the industrial process run at relatively low pressure (1–2 atm) rather than the very high pressures used in the Haber Process? (3) The rate of reaction at room temperature is negligible without a catalyst. Explain, using activation energy and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, why the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst is essential. (4) Why is 450°C chosen rather than a lower temperature that would give higher equilibrium yield? What compromise does this represent? (5) The gas from the reactor is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ (not water). Explain why water cannot be used to absorb SO₃ directly.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1a) Increasing temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH < 0). Higher temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction — the reverse — decreasing SO₃ yield. K_c decreases with temperature for exothermic reactions. (1b) Increasing pressure: 2SO₂ + O₂ = 3 mol gas → 2 mol SO₃. Higher pressure shifts equilibrium to fewer moles of gas — forward direction — increasing SO₃ yield. (1c) Adding O₂: this is adding a reactant, shifting equilibrium forward to reduce excess O₂ — increasing SO₃ yield.

(2) High pressure favours yield but carries enormous engineering costs: compressor infrastructure, high-pressure vessel construction, energy consumption, and safety risks. Unlike the Haber Process where the equilibrium yield at atmospheric pressure is too low to be economically viable (~0.05% at 450°C/1 atm), the Contact Process gives ≈99.5% conversion at 1–2 atm and 450°C — sufficient for industrial purposes. The additional yield from very high pressure does not justify the capital and operating cost. The Haber Process requires high pressure because its equilibrium yield is intrinsically low; the Contact Process does not face that constraint.

(3) At room temperature, virtually no SO₂/O₂ collisions have kinetic energy ≥ the activation energy E_a for this reaction. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution has a tail that extends beyond E_a, but at 25°C this fraction is negligible. V₂O₅ provides an alternative reaction pathway with a substantially lower activation energy — more of the area under the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve now lies beyond the new (lower) E_a, and the reaction rate becomes commercially viable. The catalyst is not consumed: SO₂ is oxidised by V₂O₅ (V⁵⁺ → V⁴⁺), then O₂ re-oxidises V⁴⁺ → V⁵⁺, regenerating the catalyst.

(4) 450°C is a compromise between rate and equilibrium yield. Lower temperature (e.g. 300°C) would give higher equilibrium yield (K_c is larger) but the rate would be so slow that the industrial reactor would be uneconomically large. Higher temperature increases rate but reduces equilibrium yield (exothermic reaction) and wastes energy. 450°C with the V₂O₅ catalyst gives ≈98% conversion with acceptable rate and reasonable energy input — the economic optimum. This is the same enthalpy/kinetics compromise seen in the Haber Process, a recurring theme in industrial chemistry.

(5) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ is highly exothermic. If SO₃ were absorbed directly into water, the reaction is so vigorous it forms a mist of tiny sulfuric acid droplets (aerosol) that is very difficult to condense or remove from the gas stream, creating a corrosive acid fog and serious yield and pollution problems. Instead, SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to form oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted with water carefully to give concentrated H₂SO₄ — a controllable, efficient process.
learningObjectives: Apply the Gibbs free energy equation (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) to predict whether a reaction is spontaneous under given conditions.
Write equilibrium constant expressions and use Le Chatelier's Principle to predict how changes in concentration, pressure, and temperature shift equilibria.
Explain reaction rates using collision theory, activation energy, and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, and describe how catalysts lower E_a.
Analyse the Haber or Contact Process as an industrial example of optimising conditions to balance kinetics and thermodynamics.
commonMistakes: Thinking a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position — catalysts lower activation energy equally for both forward and reverse reactions; equilibrium position (K) is unchanged, but equilibrium is reached faster.

Confusing the effect of temperature on rate with its effect on K — higher temperature always increases rate, but it shifts K in the endothermic direction (increases K for endothermic, decreases K for exothermic reactions).

Assuming low K means no reaction occurs — K indicates where equilibrium lies, not how fast; a reaction with very low K may still be industrially useful if products are continuously removed (Le Chatelier), e.g. the Haber Process.
Treating reaction orders as equal to stoichiometric coefficients — orders are determined by experiment, not from the balanced equation (except for elementary steps in a mechanism).
assessmentCriteria: Correctly calculates ΔG and predicts spontaneity given ΔH, ΔS, and T; identifies four thermodynamic regimes.
Writes correct K_c expressions, calculates K from equilibrium concentrations, and applies Le Chatelier's Principle to predict directional shifts.
Explains catalyst action mechanistically (alternative pathway, lower E_a) and applies Arrhenius equation conceptually to rate-temperature relationships.
Analyses a real industrial process (Haber or Contact) and justifies the compromise conditions chosen in terms of rate, yield, safety, and economics.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The relationship ΔG = −nFE connects thermodynamics to electrochemistry: n is the number of electrons transferred, F is the Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol), and E is the cell potential. This equation explains why a battery with higher voltage does more work per coulomb, and links reduction potentials (standard electrode potentials) to reaction spontaneity.

A quantum mechanical refinement of collision theory: reactions pass through a high-energy transition state (the saddle point on the potential energy surface) rather than simply requiring a collision of sufficient energy. The transition state is not an intermediate but a transient configuration at the energy maximum of the reaction coordinate. Theoretical chemistry now calculates activation energies computationally.

Biological catalysts (enzymes) follow saturation kinetics: rate = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]). At low substrate concentration [S], rate ∝ [S] (first order). At high [S], rate → V_max (zero order — all enzyme active sites are occupied). K_m (the Michaelis constant) measures enzyme-substrate affinity. This underpins pharmacology: enzyme inhibitors are often drugs.

pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) — describes the pH of a buffer solution as a function of the pKa of the weak acid and the ratio of conjugate base to acid. At the half-equivalence point of a titration, [A⁻] = [HA] so pH = pKa. Essential for blood pH regulation (carbonic acid/bicarbonate buffer, pKa ≈ 6.1, blood pH ≈ 7.4, mostly as HCO₃⁻).

In biochemistry, non-spontaneous reactions are driven by coupling them to highly spontaneous ones. ATP hydrolysis (ΔG ≈ −30 kJ/mol) is coupled to biosynthetic reactions with positive ΔG. Cells use this principle constantly — the spontaneity of ATP hydrolysis powers protein synthesis, active transport, and muscle contraction by coupling thermodynamically unfavourable processes to favourable ones.

questions.questionHtml: A reaction has ΔH = −120 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/mol·K. At what temperature (in K) does this reaction change from spontaneous to non-spontaneous?
options: The reaction is always spontaneous because ΔH is negative
questions.explanationHtml: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. The reaction is spontaneous when ΔG < 0. Crossover at ΔG = 0: 0 = ΔH − TΔS → T = ΔH/ΔS = −120,000 J/mol / −200 J/mol·K = 600 K. Below 600 K: ΔG < 0 (spontaneous, since the −ΔH term dominates). Above 600 K: ΔG > 0 (non-spontaneous — the TΔS term, which is negative since ΔS < 0, becomes large enough to overcome the negative ΔH). This is the case where both ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0: spontaneous at low temperature, non-spontaneous at high temperature.

questions.questionHtml: The Haber Process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol) is run at 450°C and 200 atm with an iron catalyst. A rival chemist proposes running at 150°C and 400 atm to increase both the equilibrium yield and the rate. Evaluate this proposal.
options: Correct — lower temperature increases both K (more NH₃ at equilibrium) and rate (more molecules have sufficient energy)

Incorrect — lower temperature does increase K (more NH₃), but it dramatically reduces rate; even with a doubled pressure and the existing catalyst, the reaction would be too slow to be commercially viable
Correct — the doubled pressure at 400 atm would more than compensate for the rate reduction from lower temperature
Incorrect — lower temperature reduces both K and rate, so the proposal is wrong on both counts
questions.correctAnswer: Incorrect — lower temperature does increase K (more NH₃), but it dramatically reduces rate; even with a doubled pressure and the existing catalyst, the reaction would be too slow to be commercially viable
questions.explanationHtml: Le Chatelier and thermodynamics: the forward reaction is exothermic, so lower temperature does shift K to favour more NH₃ — the equilibrium yield is higher at 150°C. However, the Arrhenius equation (k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)) shows that lowering temperature dramatically reduces the rate constant. At 150°C vs 450°C, the rate might be orders of magnitude slower. Even with a better catalyst, achieving commercially useful reaction rates at such low temperature has not proved feasible. The existing compromise (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst) represents decades of industrial optimisation: sufficient rate, acceptable yield (≈15% per pass), with ammonia removed continuously to drive equilibrium forward. Doubling pressure would increase both rate and yield, but 400 atm doubles the enormous engineering costs already incurred at 200 atm. The proposal correctly identifies the thermodynamic advantage of lower temperature but misunderstands the kinetic penalty.

questions.questionHtml: Diamonds are thermodynamically unstable relative to graphite at room temperature and pressure (ΔG < 0 for diamond → graphite). Yet diamonds persist essentially forever under normal conditions. A student concludes: "ΔG must actually be positive for diamond → graphite at room temperature, since it clearly doesn't happen." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing — the student is correct; thermodynamic data showing ΔG < 0 for this transition must be wrong

The student confuses thermodynamic spontaneity with kinetic feasibility. ΔG < 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favourable (the products are more stable), but says nothing about the rate. The activation energy for rearranging diamond's crystal structure is enormous; without sufficient energy to cross this barrier, the reaction does not proceed on any human timescale
The student is partially correct — ΔG is negative but only barely, making the reaction spontaneous but extremely slow
Thermodynamic stability is irrelevant for solids — only gases and liquids can be thermodynamically unstable
questions.correctAnswer: The student confuses thermodynamic spontaneity with kinetic feasibility. ΔG < 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favourable (the products are more stable), but says nothing about the rate. The activation energy for rearranging diamond's crystal structure is enormous; without sufficient energy to cross this barrier, the reaction does not proceed on any human timescale
questions.explanationHtml: This is the classic example distinguishing thermodynamics from kinetics. ΔG < 0 for diamond → graphite means graphite is the more stable allotrope at ambient conditions — thermodynamics says the reaction should happen. But thermodynamics tells you the direction of spontaneous change and the equilibrium position; it says nothing about the rate at which equilibrium is approached. The rate is governed by the activation energy E_a, which for disrupting diamond's covalent crystal lattice is enormous — no C−C bonds break spontaneously at room temperature. Diamond is kinetically stable (metastable) but thermodynamically unstable. The same principle applies throughout chemistry: many thermodynamically favourable reactions are kinetically inert. H₂ + O₂ → H₂O is highly spontaneous (ΔG ≪ 0) but the mixture is stable until ignited — the activation energy prevents spontaneous reaction at room temperature.
